50915: If God is good and powerful, why is there so much evil and pain? The question, the Bible's own answers and protests, the main Christian and Jewish responses, and how to stay with people who suffer
50916: Theodicy is the attempt to show that God is just and good even though the world is full of evil and suffering; a 'defence' aims at less, showing only that God and evil are not logically contradictory. The problem is ancient and sharp: if God is fully good, fully powerful and fully knowing, why does he allow children to die of cancer, tsunamis to drown villages and people to torture one another? The Bible does not hide from this question. It contains whole books of protest (Job, Lamentations, Habakkuk), prayers that accuse God (Ps 88), and Jesus himself crying 'My God, why have you forsaken me?' (Mark 15:34). Christians and Jews have given many serious answers: evil comes from misused freedom, suffering can grow souls, God has reasons we cannot see, the world is a battlefield with real enemies, God suffers with us on the cross, and God will finally wipe away every tear (Rev 21:4). No answer removes all the difficulty, and the Bible itself warns against neat explanations offered to people in pain (Job 42:7). Most wise teachers hold the explanations loosely and the sufferer closely: lament, presence and hope come first, arguments second.
50917: The problem is usually stated as an 'inconsistent triad': God is all-powerful, God is wholly good, and evil exists. Every response either denies that the three really conflict or adjusts how one of them is understood.
50918: Philosophers separate the logical problem (God and evil cannot both exist) from the evidential problem (the amount and kind of evil make God unlikely). Many philosophers, including many atheists, think Alvin Plantinga's free-will defence answered the logical form; the evidential form, pressed by William Rowe in 1979, is still widely debated.
50919: The Bible rejects the simple rule that suffering always proves sin: God rebukes Job's friends (Job 42:7) and Jesus denies that the man born blind or the victims at Siloam were worse sinners (John 9:1-3, Luke 13:1-5).
50920: Lament is not a lack of faith. About a third of the Psalms are complaints addressed to God, and the tradition of arguing with God runs from Abraham (Gen 18:25) and Moses (Exod 32:11-14) to Jewish thinkers after the Holocaust.
50921: The main Christian responses (Augustinian, soul-making, free will, Reformed sovereignty, cosmic conflict, skeptical theism, open theism, process, cruciform) disagree about God's power, knowledge and control. Each has real strengths and real costs.
50922: The New Testament answer is less an explanation than a story: God enters suffering in Jesus, defeats evil through the cross and resurrection, and promises a renewed creation where death is no more (Rom 8:18-25, 1 Cor 15:26, Rev 21:1-5).
50923: Related problems include divine hiddenness, hell, violence in the Old Testament and animal suffering before humans existed; each sharpens the main question in a different way.
50924: Pastorally, presence comes before explanation. Job's friends did best in their first seven silent days (Job 2:13). 'Everything happens for a reason' and 'you must not have enough faith' wound people and are not biblical teaching.
50931: The map of the problem of evil
50932: Start with the triad in the centre. Red-toned nodes state the problem in its different forms; the others are the main responses from Scripture, Christian tradition, philosophy and Jewish thought. Follow the arrows to see what answers what, what grows out of what, and where views clash. No single node is 'the answer'; most thoughtful believers combine several.
50935: Three claims that seem unable to be true together: God is all-powerful, God is perfectly good, and evil exists. Lactantius reports Epicurus framing it this way, and David Hume restated it. Every theodicy is an attempt to show the three are consistent, or to refine what one of them means.
50939: The claim that God and evil are strictly contradictory, so belief in God is irrational. J. L. Mackie pressed this in 'Evil and Omnipotence' (1955). The argument needs a hidden premise: that a good, powerful God would always eliminate evil. Critics of the argument ask whether that premise is necessarily true.
50943: The weaker but stronger-feeling claim: the amount and kind of evil make God's existence improbable. William Rowe (1979) imagined a fawn trapped in a forest fire, burned and dying for days with no one to see it. Such suffering seems pointless, and a good God would not allow pointless suffering.
50948: Evil done by free agents: murder, cruelty, injustice, abuse, war. The Bible traces it to the human heart and to the misuse of the freedom God gave (Gen 4:6-8, Jer 17:9). It is the easiest kind to connect to the free-will response.
50950: Suffering that no human chose: earthquakes, tsunamis, disease, birth defects, famine. It is harder to blame on human freedom. Responses link it to the Fall, to fixed natural laws, to fallen spiritual powers, or to a creation that is good but not yet finished.
50952: Evil that serves no greater good at all. If even one such evil exists, many argue, God cannot be both good and powerful. Theists either deny that any evil is truly pointless (skeptical theism, Reformed view) or argue that God may permit some pointless evil as the cost of a world with real freedom and stable laws (open theism, some free-will views).
50954: Marilyn McCord Adams' term for evils so terrible that they seem to destroy the meaning of a person's life, such as a parent forced to harm their own child. She argued that general 'greater good' arguments are not enough; God must defeat such evils within each victim's own life, finally through union with God.
50959: A related problem: if a loving God exists, why do many sincere seekers find no sign of him? J. L. Schellenberg argued in 1993 that a perfectly loving God would always make a relationship available to anyone not resisting it. The Bible itself speaks of God hiding his face.
50961: Fossils show predation, disease and extinction for millions of years before humans. This troubles theodicies that blame all suffering on human sin. Responses include a cosmic fall of angelic powers, a 'cost of an evolving world' view, or a reading of Genesis in which death among animals was not the 'death' brought by sin.
50963: A blameless man loses everything after the accuser questions his motives. His friends insist he must have sinned; Job protests his innocence and demands a hearing. God answers from the whirlwind with questions about creation, never explaining the heavenly wager, then says the friends were wrong and Job spoke rightly.
50965: The Bible gives sufferers words to complain to God: 'How long, O Lord?' (Ps 13:1). Lament is covenant speech: it holds God to his promises. Ps 88 ends in darkness without resolution, which tells sufferers that even unresolved prayer belongs in Scripture.
50967: The principle that the righteous prosper and the wicked suffer. It is true as a covenant pattern (Deut 28) and in Proverbs, but Job, Ecclesiastes and Jesus deny that it works as a rule for reading individual lives. Misused, it becomes the idea that every sufferer deserves it.
50969: Jesus refuses to link specific disasters to specific sins (Luke 13:1-5, John 9:1-3). He weeps at a tomb (John 11:35), heals as a sign of God's kingdom pushing back evil (Luke 13:16), and calls all people to repentance in the face of life's fragility.
50971: For Christians, the centre of any answer. The worst moral evil in the story, the murder of the innocent Son, is both freely done by wicked people and within God's saving plan (Acts 2:23). On the cross God does not explain suffering from a distance but enters it.
50973: The promise that present suffering is not the last word. Creation groans like a woman in labour waiting for renewal (Rom 8:18-25). Death will be destroyed (1 Cor 15:26) and God will wipe every tear (Rev 21:4). Many think no theodicy works without this horizon.
50976: Augustine taught that God made everything good and that evil is not a 'thing' but a lack or twisting of good, like blindness in an eye. Evil entered through the free rebellion of angels and humans; natural disorder follows the Fall. God permits evil only because he can bring greater good out of it.
50981: Following hints in Irenaeus, John Hick (1966) argued that humans were made immature and placed in a challenging world at an 'epistemic distance' from God, so that they could freely grow into children of God. A world without pain could not produce courage, compassion or trust.
50987: Alvin Plantinga argued that a world with creatures who are truly free to do good is more valuable than a world of puppets, and that it is possible even God could not create such a world without some of them choosing evil. If that is even possible, the logical problem fails.
50990: God ordains everything that happens, including evil acts, without himself doing evil; human agents remain responsible (compatibilism). Joseph's words are the key text: 'you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good' (Gen 50:20). Evil is never pointless because God has a good purpose for every event.
50992: Gottfried Leibniz, who coined the word 'theodicy' (1710), argued that a perfect God must create the best possible world, so this one, with its evils, is the best whole. After the Lisbon earthquake of 1755 Voltaire mocked the idea in *Candide*.
50996: The world is a battlefield. Real spiritual powers who freely rebelled against God oppress creation, and Jesus came to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8). Much evil is not God's will at all but the work of enemies whose defeat began at the cross. Greg Boyd is a leading modern voice.
51001: If God exists, we should expect not to see many of his reasons, just as an infant cannot see the reasons for a vaccination. So 'I cannot see a reason' does not show 'there is no reason'. Stephen Wykstra (1984) and Michael Bergmann developed this as a reply to Rowe.
51005: God knows everything that can be known, but the future free choices of creatures are not yet settled and so not yet knowable. God takes real risks in creating free beings. Specific evils may be genuinely pointless and grieve God, who works to bring good out of them.
51010: God's power is persuasive, not coercive. God cannot unilaterally stop evil, because every creature has some power of its own. God lures the world toward good and suffers with it. This removes the problem of why God does not intervene, at the cost of a much more limited God.
51016: Luther taught that God is known most truly in weakness and suffering, not in displays of glory. Jürgen Moltmann (*The Crucified God*, 1972) argued that God himself suffers the godforsakenness of the cross. The answer to suffering is a suffering God who shares it from inside and overcomes it.
51020: Classical theology (impassibility) says God is not overwhelmed or changed by suffering; the Son suffered in his human nature. Many modern theologians (passibility) say a loving God must truly feel grief. Both sides affirm that in Christ God truly entered human suffering.
51023: In Dostoevsky's novel (1880), Ivan does not deny God; he refuses the deal. No future harmony could justify the tears of one tortured child, so he 'returns his ticket'. Dostoevsky answers not with an argument but with the life of Father Zosima and Alyosha's active love.
51028: A deep Jewish tradition of holding God to his own justice. Abraham asks, 'Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?' (Gen 18:25). Moses pleads against God's wrath. Rabbinic stories, Yiddish prayers and Wiesel's *The Trial of God* continue it. Protest is an act of faith in God's covenant, not a rejection of it.
51032: After six million Jews were murdered, Jewish thinkers divided. Richard Rubenstein rejected the God who acts in history; Emil Fackenheim named a '614th commandment' not to give Hitler posthumous victories; Eliezer Berkovits spoke of God hiding his face; Hans Jonas proposed a God who gave up power. Elie Wiesel kept faith and protest together.
51039: Rabbi Harold Kushner, after his son died of a rare ageing disease, wrote *When Bad Things Happen to Good People* (1981). He concluded that God is good but does not control everything; God does not send tragedy but gives strength to bear it. The book comforted millions and was criticised for shrinking God.
51043: Most pastoral wisdom says: sit with sufferers, weep with them, and do not hurry to explain. Job's friends were wise for seven silent days and foolish once they started to explain. Paul says God comforts us so we can comfort others.
51044: Nicholas Wolterstorff, Lament for a Son
51048: In India, suffering is often explained by karma: the results of deeds in this or past lives. This resembles the retribution theology of Job's friends. The gospel answer stresses grace: suffering is not a simple payment for past deeds, and God's mercy is not earned. Christians should speak of this respectfully, knowing that Hindu traditions also teach grace (for example in Tamil Saiva and Vaishnava devotion).
51074: shares confidence in a plan with
51095: Walking through evil and suffering: a path for thinking and praying
51096: Use this path when you face a real evil, your own or someone else's, or when you study a hard passage about suffering. The order matters: it moves from honesty, to prayer, to careful thought, to action and hope. Many people jump straight to step 7 (explanations) and skip the rest; the Bible does not.
51098: Say plainly what happened and that it is wrong. The Bible never calls evil good. Jesus was 'deeply moved' and angry at death before he raised Lazarus. Do not rush to soften the harm with religious phrases.
51099: What exactly happened, and who was harmed?
51100: Am I tempted to say it was 'not so bad' to protect God or myself?
51101: What would I call this if it happened to a stranger?
51103: Is this moral evil (someone chose it), natural evil (disease, disaster), or both? Is it horrendous, the kind that threatens to destroy a life's meaning? Different responses fit different kinds, and mixing them up causes harm, for example blaming a cancer patient for their illness.
51104: Did a human or group choose this, or did it come through nature?
51105: Is there injustice here that needs to be named and resisted?
51106: Does this evil seem to have any possible good outcome, or does it seem pointless?
51108: There is the intellectual question ('How can God allow this?') and the personal one ('Where is God for me now?'). C. S. Lewis wrote one book on each: *The Problem of Pain* (1940) and, after his wife died, *A Grief Observed* (1961). A grieving person usually needs the second kind of help first.
51109: Is the person asking for an argument, or for help to survive?
51110: Am I answering a question that was not asked?
51111: What does the sufferer need from me today?
51112: Bring it to God in lament
51113: Biblical lament usually has a shape: address God, complain honestly, ask for help, state trust, and sometimes promise praise. But Ps 88 has almost none of that and is still Scripture. You are allowed to say 'How long?' and 'Why?'. This is covenant faith speaking, not unbelief.
51114: What do I actually want to say to God, without editing?
51115: Which psalm says what I feel (Ps 13, 22, 44, 88)?
51116: Can I keep talking to God even if I am angry with him?
51118: Ask whether an explanation repeats the mistake of Job's friends: assuming suffering proves sin, or that God owes success to the faithful. Jesus rejects that reasoning. Also ask whether it makes God the author of sin, or so weak that he cannot save.
51119: Does this explanation blame the victim?
51120: Would God say of this explanation what he said to Eliphaz (Job 42:7)?
51121: Does it fit the character of God shown in Jesus?
51122: Does it still let me call evil evil?
51124: The cross does not explain every evil, but it shows three things: God is not distant from suffering; God can bring salvation through the worst evil without approving it; and evil does not have the last word. Christians read every other suffering in that light.
51125: What does it mean that God's Son cried 'why have you forsaken me'?
51126: How can the cross be both a great crime and God's plan (Acts 2:23)?
51127: What does the resurrection say about this situation?
51129: Now compare the theodicies: free will, soul-making, sovereignty, cosmic conflict, skeptical theism, and others. Ask what each says about this specific evil. Most wise believers draw on several and admit that some mystery remains.
51130: Which response best explains this kind of evil?
51131: What does each response cost (God's power, goodness, or our understanding)?
51132: Where must I say 'I do not know'?
51134: The Bible's main response to evil is not a theory but resistance: heal, feed, protect, seek justice, forgive. Jesus treated sickness and oppression as enemies to defeat. Theodicy that leads to passivity has gone wrong.
51135: What practical help is needed now?
51136: Is there an injustice I should oppose?
51137: Where can my own suffering make me more able to comfort others?
51139: The final answer in Scripture is the renewal of all things. Paul does not call present suffering small; he says it is not worth comparing with the glory to come. Hope does not cancel grief; it lets us 'grieve, but not as those who have no hope'.
51140: What does God promise about the end of this suffering?
51141: How do Rom 8 and Rev 21 change how I see today?
51142: Who can hold hope for me when I cannot hold it myself?
51143: Which response to evil fits your convictions?
51144: This tree helps you see where your existing beliefs about God and the world lead. It does not tell you which view is true. If you are in pain right now, take the first branch; the arguments can wait.
51145: What brings you to this question right now?
51146: I or someone close to me is suffering now
51147: I want to think through the intellectual problem
51148: I am troubled by a specific Bible passage or event
51149: What do you need most at this moment?
51150: Words to speak to God, even angry ones
51151: To know God is with me in this
51152: To know this will not last forever
51153: What kind of text troubles you?
51154: A text where God seems to send disaster or evil (Isa 45:7, Amos 3:6)
51155: A text that says the righteous always prosper
51156: Violence commanded in the Old Testament
51157: Does God decide every event that happens, including each evil act?
51158: Yes: nothing happens outside God's specific plan
51159: No: God allows creatures real freedom that he does not control
51160: Then does God have a good purpose for every evil, even if we cannot see it?
51161: Yes, and Scripture shows enough of it to trust him
51162: Yes, but we usually cannot see it at all
51163: Does God know every future free choice before it happens?
51164: Yes, God knows the whole future
51165: No, the free future is open and not yet knowable
51166: Why did God give freedom that leads to evil?
51167: Because love and goodness require real freedom
51168: Because character is formed by struggle
51169: Because spiritual powers also have freedom, and they rebelled
51170: Could God stop any evil he wanted to stop, if he chose to?
51172: No, God's power is persuasive, not controlling
51173: I cannot answer, and I want to protest
51175: Pray the lament psalms out loud: Ps 13 if you feel forgotten, Ps 22 if you feel abandoned, Ps 44 if you feel faithful yet punished, Ps 88 if you have no words of hope left. The Bible gives you permission to complain to God. Find one person who will listen without explaining.
51176: The God who suffers with you
51177: Christians believe God has been inside human suffering in Jesus: rejected, tortured, abandoned, killed. He does not ask you to suffer anything he refused to share. Read the passion story slowly, and the promise that we have a high priest who sympathises with our weakness. This is the heart of the theology of the cross.
51178: Scripture promises a day when God will wipe away every tear and death will be no more. Paul, who suffered greatly, calls present troubles 'light and momentary' only when compared with that coming glory. Hope does not deny grief; it holds it within a larger story.
51179: Let wisdom books correct each other
51180: Proverbs gives general patterns (wise living tends to go well). Job and Ecclesiastes show the exceptions: the righteous can suffer and the wicked can prosper. The Bible holds these together on purpose. Read Prov 3 alongside Job 21 and Ps 73.
51181: See the course lesson on hard texts
51182: Violence in the Old Testament is a related but separate problem. The app's course lesson 'Hard Texts: Violence, Accommodation and Changing Perception' sets out the main ways of reading these passages (hyperbole in ancient war language, accommodation, progressive revelation, the Jesus lens) and their critiques.
51184: Your answers fit the Reformed view (Calvin, Westminster Confession, D. A. Carson, John Piper): God ordains all things, including evil acts, for good ends, while humans remain responsible and God is not the author of sin. Its comfort is that no suffering is wasted. Its hardest question is how God is not responsible for evil he decrees. Read the critiques of this view as well.
51185: Your answers fit skeptical theism (Stephen Wykstra, Michael Bergmann): the gap between God's mind and ours means we should not expect to see God's reasons. This is a defence, not a full theodicy. Critics say it makes it hard to judge anything as good or bad. It is held both by Reformed and non-Reformed thinkers.
51186: Your answers fit open theism (Clark Pinnock, John Sanders, William Hasker, Greg Boyd): God created a world with a genuinely open future, took a risk, and does not plan each evil. Some evils are truly pointless and grieve God. Its strength is that God is never the author of a child's murder. Critics say it weakens God's knowledge and the certainty of his promises.
